absent: Behavior of core queue and activation helpers, pool kicking, pending grab and disabled clearing, and work assignment and processing loops.
Full object layouts for queues, pool queues, pools, workers, and delayed and RCU work, plus concurrency limits and teardown ordering.
Numeric values of idle and mayday intervals, creation cooldown, batch limits, nice levels, and default minima.
Timer, RCU barrier, CPU mask, housekeeping, and scheduler interactions owned by other dossiers.
Synchronous cancel and flush internals, barrier wait paths, and per-CPU scheduling guarantees.
Lock dependency map contents and bottom-half worker execution details.
Allocation failure handling beyond the attribute and node paths shown.
Rescuer wakeup and stop coordination with queue teardown.

findings.text: Public delayed queue entry takes a cpu selector plus workqueue plus delayed work plus delay and reports whether the item was newly queued. It guards the pending bit under saved interrupt state and skips queueing when the item was already pending or is disabled.

Modify entry grabs any pending state of the delayed item, re-arms it on the given cpu and queue with the new delay unless disabled, restores interrupt state, and returns whether prior pending state existed.

Timer callback derives its delayed work from the expiring timer and queues the inner work on the recorded cpu and queue. The fragment notes an expectation of interrupt-safe timer context with interrupts already off.
RCU callback derives its container work and queues it as unbound while interrupts are disabled across the queue operation, then re-enables them.

Delayed queue helper treats zero delay as immediate queue with no timer use for both speed and tick granularity reasons. For nonzero delay it records queue and cpu in the delayed item, sets expiry as current jiffies plus delay, and arms the timer.

Timer placement prefers a housekeeping cpu when that facility is enabled, falling back to any housekeeping cpu if the current one is unsuitable. Otherwise unbound items use a global timer path while bound items use a per-cpu timer path.

Delayed helper warns once if timer callback identity is unexpected, if timer already pending, if work linkage is non-empty, or if a bound cpu is offline, indicating caller contract violations rather than handling them.
Unplug path requires the queue mutex held on entry and serializes the oldest pool queue under its pool interrupt-safe spinlock while clearing the plugged state and activating work.

While plugged, queueing is described as skipping activation including active count and pending list accounting. Unplug restores both by activating the first inactive item and, when more inactives remain, enqueueing on the pending list, then kicking the pool.

Detach serializes under the pool attach mutex, clears the worker pool association while holding it, and clears unbound and rebound flags only after detachment without pool lock. Worker process flag updates for the current task also hold the attach mutex.
Detaching a bottom-half pool worker triggers a once warning because one permanent bottom-half worker per cpu is expected never to detach.

Idle timeout handler exits early if cull work is already pending. Otherwise under pool lock it checks for surplus workers via the most recently idled entry in last-in-first-out order, compares current time against last activity plus idle timeout, rearms the idle timer when not yet expired, and outside the lock queues cull work on the system default queue when expiry is reached.

Cull takes the attach mutex outside the pool interrupt-safe spinlock, drains expired idle workers from the tail while surplus remains, rearms the idle timer on first unexpired entry, then releases pool lock before detaching dying workers and finally reaps them after dropping the attach mutex.

Holding the attach mutex across the dying-mark phase is described as preventing an already running worker from passing its worker-mark step in a self-destruct path after being marked but before detachment.

Mayday distress handling requires the global mayday spinlock held for list changes. The pool timeout nests pool lock outside mayday lock. Rescuer takes mayday lock for list drain, drops it across pool attach and work processing, and retakes it.

Distress send ignores queues without a rescuer, and for a pool queue not already on distress pins it with a reference, appends it to the queue distress list, wakes the rescuer task, and increments a mayday counter. The pool timer only walks the work list sending distress when worker creation is still needed, then rearms after a fixed interval.

Worker creation helper releases the pool lock across its blocking section. It arms the mayday timer with an initial timeout, repeatedly attempts creation with interruptible cooldown sleep while creation is still needed, synchronously deletes the timer, reacquires the pool lock, and restarts if creation is again needed because state may have changed while unlocked.

Manager election uses a manager-active flag to ensure at most one manager. The winner records itself as manager, runs the creation helper, clears itself and the flag, then wakes manager waiters and reports that it managed.

Worker main loop marks itself as workqueue worker, then under pool lock checks a die flag and on death drops the lock, clears the worker mark, nulls its pool link, frees its identifier and exits. Otherwise it leaves idle, sleeps when no more workers are needed, enters management when starting is blocked, validates its scheduled list is empty, clears preparation and rebound participation flags, then repeatedly takes the head of the pool work list and processes assigned work while continuation is indicated. When no work remains it sets preparation, enters idle, sets an idle task state while still holding the pool lock to avoid lost wakeups, releases the lock, schedules, and resumes at the top.

Rescuer sets a rescuer nice level and permanent worker mark with preparation never cleared so it stays outside concurrency management. Each pass records stop intent, drains the queue distress list under mayday lock by unlinking each entry, attaching to its pool, warning if its own scheduled list is non-empty, and processing rescued items. It enforces a per-turn batch limit by requeueing distress when other queues wait and work remains, removes any leftover rescue cursor when no distress remains, kicks the pool to restore concurrency before detaching, drops the distress reference, and after the list empties exits on stop with running state and cleared worker mark or otherwise schedules idle and repeats.

Rescue selection returns false when the pool queue has no active count. When creation is not needed it normally returns false, except it continues while manager activity suggests lingering memory pressure and no other queue needs help. Otherwise it scans the pool work list from start or from a saved cursor, assigns the first item belonging to the target queue, increments a rescued counter, moves the cursor behind the successor, and reports success.
Drain helper object for dead-cpu bottom-half pools groups a work item with a target pool pointer and a completion used to signal finish.

Dead-cpu drain marks the pool as draining under pool lock because the dead cpu cannot be kicked and execution will nest, runs the bottom-half worker for its first worker, clears the mark, and checks for remaining work. If more remains it requeues itself on a high priority or normal system bottom-half queue based on pool niceness to avoid hogging the cpu, else it signals completion.
Barrier object groups a work item with a completion plus an informational task pointer. Its work function completes the completion to wake a waiter.

Delayed flush disables interrupts, synchronously deletes the timer and if deletion found it pending queues the inner work on its recorded cpu and queue, re-enables interrupts, then flushes the inner work. RCU flush checks the pending bit and when set issues an RCU barrier before flushing and reports true, otherwise only flushes.

Cancel and disable family are thin wrappers selecting plain, delayed, synchronous, and disabling variants by combining delayed and disable option bits when delegating to shared cancel helpers. Enable for delayed work delegates to the shared work enable helper.

Per-cpu runner allocates per-cpu work storage failing with out-of-memory, holds the cpu read lock, initializes and schedules one work per online cpu with the supplied function, flushes each per-cpu work, then releases the lock, frees storage, and returns success.

Process-context helper runs the supplied function directly on the supplied execute container and returns zero when not in interrupt, otherwise initializes the container work with the function, schedules it on the system queue, and returns one to indicate deferral.

Attribute allocator zero-allocates the attribute object plus two cpu masks, copies the possible mask into the main mask, sets a default affinity scope, and on any allocation failure frees via the shared attribute free helper and returns null.

Lock dependency support has enabled and disabled builds. Enabled build registers a key, builds a completion-prefixed name with fallback to the queue name, and initializes the queue lock map. Unregister and free are guarded on map identity with key unregister and conditional name free. Disabled build provides empty init, unregister, and free.

Per-node active accounting allocates one counter object per node plus a fallback slot at the node-count index, each zero-allocated on its node and initialized with a default minimum, zero atomic count, lock init, and empty pending list. Free walks all nodes plus fallback freeing and nulling each.

Deferred reclamation via RCU frees queue state by conditionally freeing node accounting for unbound queues, then lock dependency state, per-cpu queue pointers, attributes, and the queue itself. Pool reclamation destroys the worker identifier allocator, frees attributes, and frees the pool.

Delayed queue, modify, RCU queue, and delayed flush paths hold interrupts disabled or saved across pending-bit manipulation and queue or timer operations, restoring or enabling afterward to serialize against timer and RCU contexts.

The fragments use a value for unbound cpu handling named WORK_CPU_UNBOUND and a bit index for pending state named WORK_STRUCT_PENDING_BIT and option bits for delayed cancel named WORK_CANCEL_DELAYED and for disabling named WORK_CANCEL_DISABLE and a flag for unbound queues named WQ_UNBOUND and a default affinity scope named WQ_AFFN_DFL and a default minimum activity named WQ_DFL_MIN_ACTIVE.

The fragments use pool role flags named POOL_BH and POOL_BH_DRAINING and POOL_MANAGER_ACTIVE and worker lifecycle flags named WORKER_UNBOUND and WORKER_REBOUND and WORKER_PREP and WORKER_DIE and WORKER_NOT_RUNNING and a process flag named PF_WQ_WORKER and task states named TASK_IDLE and TASK_RUNNING.

The fragments use rescuer tuning named RESCUER_NICE_LEVEL and RESCUER_BATCH and timing intervals named IDLE_WORKER_TIMEOUT and MAYDAY_INTERVAL and MAYDAY_INITIAL_TIMEOUT and CREATE_COOLDOWN and a high priority niceness named HIGHPRI_NICE_LEVEL and statistic indexes named PWQ_STAT_MAYDAY and PWQ_STAT_RESCUED and allocation facts named NUMA_NO_NODE and GFP_KERNEL and ENOMEM.

Rescuer bounds consecutive work per queue by a batch constant and when exceeded with other distress pending and active work plus creation need still true it re-sends distress under mayday lock and moves on. It guarantees the rescue cursor is not left linked when its queue has no distress entry. Worker and rescuer paths warn once if the scheduled list is non-empty where empty is expected.
